title: I use Gemini Notebook regularly, but these underrated features deserve more attention
excerpt: They make research so much easier
content_html:
Published Nov 24, 2026, 8:04 AM EST

I cover Android with a focus on productivity, automation, and Google’s ecosystem, including Gemini and everyday apps. With a background in engineering and software development, I tend to go beyond surface-level tips.
Before joining AP, I wrote for tech publications such as Gizbot in 2023 and iJunkie (formerly known as iPhoneHacks) from 2021 to 2022.

I use Gemini Notebook regularly to organize research and explore ideas. It is one of those tools I keep coming back to, but it's not only about asking questions about uploaded documents or generating audio overviews.

Some lesser-known features can make working with information much easier, yet they're easy to overlook.

Here are a few underrated Gemini Notebook features worth exploring, especially if you use it regularly.

Automatically organize sources with labels

Sort your research by topic

As I add more sources to a Gemini Notebook, finding a document or reference can become a chore. Instead of scrolling through a long, unorganized list, I use automatic source labeling to group related material by topic.

If a notebook has at least five sources, Gemini Notebook can analyze the contents and automatically organize them into relevant categories.

To use it, open the Sources panel on the left and click the Auto-label sources by topic icon above the source list. Gemini Notebook will analyze your sources and create expandable groups based on their content.

You can rename labels, personalize them with emojis, or move sources into different categories if the automatic organization isn't quite right. You can also create your own labels to organize sources the way you prefer.

Labels aren't only for keeping the sidebar tidy. You can select a category to limit Gemini Notebook's chat responses to sources under that label.

For instance, if I'm researching a topic with background reading, reference documents, and guides, I can select only the guides when I want answers based on those sources. This keeps the conversation focused without requiring me to remove unrelated documents from the notebook.

Find and add research sources without leaving your notebook

Find relevant articles and Drive files in one place

One feature I find useful in Gemini Notebook is that I don't have to leave my notebook to find more research materials.

I can search the web for new sources or find documents I've saved in Google Drive, all from the same interface.

To use it, open the Sources panel on the left and enter a question in the search box. You'll see options to search Web or Drive.

Choose Web to find relevant articles, web pages, and other online material, or switch to Drive to look for existing Google Docs, Sheets, Slides, and other files.

There's also a Deep Research option for more extensive online research. It browses hundreds of websites and compiles its findings into a detailed report.

Drive sources sync with their original files, so changes in Google Drive are reflected in the notebook without importing the documents.

Save useful chat responses as notes

Build a collection of useful insights

When Gemini Notebook gives me a useful answer, I save individual responses as notes and keep them handy for future reference.

To do this, click Save to note (pin icon) below the response. Gemini Notebook pins it to the source panel, where I can access it alongside my other notes and research materials.

The saved note retains the original formatting, including tables and clickable citations, so I don't lose the references behind an answer.

There's another useful trick: saved notes can become sources. Gemini Notebook can use them when answering future questions, and they can provide context when generating Audio Overviews and Study Guides.

So, if I save an explanation or research summary, I can build on it in later sessions rather than starting from scratch.

You can also create your own notes using Create note in the Sources panel, which is handy for adding personal observations, reminders, or information Gemini Notebook hasn't covered.

Use Mind Maps to see how your sources connect

Turn complex topics into visual maps

One of my favorite ways to get a better overview of my research is to use Gemini Notebook's Mind Maps feature. Instead of scrolling through a long list of sources or reading summaries one by one, I turn the information into an interactive visual map.

To create one, open a notebook and select Mind Map in the Studio panel.

This is useful when researching a topic with several moving parts. For example, if I'm collecting articles about Android security, a mind map can help me see how permissions, app tracking, malware, encryption, and privacy settings fit into the bigger picture.

I can expand individual branches to explore smaller topics or collapse them for a cleaner overview.

The best part is that the map is interactive. Clicking a node lets me ask Gemini Notebook follow-up questions about that subject without formulating a completely new query.

If I'm researching a new topic, I can select an unfamiliar concept and ask for a simple explanation or examples from my sources.

You can also download the finished mind map as an image to keep or share.

Unlock more of Gemini Notebook's research tools

I get plenty of use out of Gemini Notebook for researching topics, but its value goes beyond answering questions.

Features like saved notes, built-in source discovery, and Mind Maps make it easier to organize information and turn research into something useful. You can also find additional research on the web or in Google Drive without leaving your notebook.
